title: Οἶνος καὶ Οὖτις
titleEn: The Wine and the Name of Nobody — Odyssey 9.281–370
part: The Wine and the Name of Nobody (9.281–370)
about: Odysseus, still telling his story at the Phaeacian court, answers the Cyclops' question about his ship with an invented wreck. The Cyclops gives no answer but seizes two more of the men and eats them, and Odysseus, horrified and helpless, thinks of stabbing him as he lies stretched out, full of his meal, but sees that they would then never be able to move the stone from the doorway. At dawn the Cyclops milks his flocks, eats two more men, and drives the flocks out, closing the door behind him as easily as a lid on a quiver. Odysseus prepares his revenge: he cuts a length from the Cyclops' green olive club, has it trimmed smooth, sharpens the tip and hardens it in the fire, hides it in the dung, and has four companions chosen by lot to help him use it. When the Cyclops comes home at evening and eats two more, Odysseus offers him a bowl of dark wine. He drinks it with delight and asks for a second cup, and Odysseus gives him three; then, promising a guest-gift, he asks Odysseus' name. Odysseus says that his name is Nobody, and the Cyclops answers that he will eat Nobody last, and that this will be his guest-gift.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο πειράζων, ἐμὲ δ’ οὐ λάθεν εἰδότα πολλά,
ἀλλά μιν ἄψορρον προσέφην δολίοις ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, testing, but me it did not escape, knowing many things,
but him in return I addressed with guileful words:
sentences.i: So he spoke, putting me to the test, but it did not escape me, who knew much, and I addressed him in return with guileful words:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο 'so he spoke' closes the Cyclops' question about where the ship lay, and πειράζων 'testing' tells us Odysseus took it for a probe. ἐμὲ δ’ οὐ λάθεν is 'and it did not escape me': λανθάνω takes the person who fails to notice in the accusative, and εἰδότα πολλά 'knowing many things' agrees with ἐμέ. ἄψορρον 'back again, in return' is an adjective used as an adverb. δολίοις ἐπέεσσι is 'with guileful words', the dative plural of ἔπος in its uncontracted -εσσι form. The ano teleia opens Odysseus' reply, spoken inside his own telling and so in single quotation marks.

sentences.t:
νέα μέν μοι κατέαξε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων
πρὸς πέτρῃσι βαλὼν ὑμῆς ἐπὶ πείρασι γαίης,
ἄκρῃ προσπελάσας· ἄνεμος δ’ ἐκ πόντου ἔνεικεν·
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ σὺν τοῖσδε ὑπέκφυγον αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l:
‘A ship, for me, Poseidon earth-shaker shattered,
having hurled it against rocks at the borders of your land,
having driven it close to a headland; and a wind from the sea carried it;
but I with these here escaped steep destruction.’
sentences.i: ‘Poseidon, the earth-shaker, shattered my ship, hurling it against the rocks at the borders of your land and driving it up to a headland, and a wind carried it in from the sea; but I escaped steep destruction, together with these men.’
sentences.n: This is the invented wreck with which Odysseus answers the Cyclops, in single quotation marks inside his own telling. νέα is a form of ναῦς 'ship', the object of κατέαξε, the aorist of κατάγνυμι 'break in pieces'; μέν 'on the one hand' looks forward to αὐτὰρ ἐγώ 'but I' in the last line. Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων is the subject, with the participles βαλών 'having hurled' and προσπελάσας 'having driven close', the second taking the dative ἄκρῃ 'to a headland'. ὑμῆς is the feminine genitive of ὑμός 'your' (plural), agreeing with γαίης, Ionic for γῆς; πείρασι is the dative plural of πεῖραρ 'limit, end'. ὑπέκφυγον 'I escaped' has no augment (the ε belongs to the preposition ἐκ), and σὺν τοῖσδε 'with these here' points to the companions beside him.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ οὐδὲν ἀμείβετο νηλέι θυμῷ,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἀναΐξας ἑτάροις ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἴαλλε,
σὺν δὲ δύω μάρψας ὥς τε σκύλακας ποτὶ γαίῃ
κόπτ’·
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and he me nothing answered with pitiless heart,
but he, springing up, upon my companions hands laid,
and two together seizing, like puppies, against the ground
struck them;
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he gave me no answer, with a pitiless heart; instead he sprang up and laid hands on my companions, and seizing two together he struck them against the ground like puppies;
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην 'so I spoke' is the first-person counterpart of ὣς ἔφατο, and ὁ δέ 'and he' has ὁ as a pronoun; οὐδὲν ἀμείβετο is 'he answered nothing', with ἀμείβετο unaugmented and νηλέι θυμῷ 'with pitiless heart' a dative of manner. ὅ γε is again 'he'; ἀναΐξας is the aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω 'spring up', and ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἴαλλε, from ἰάλλω 'send, throw', is the idiom 'laid hands upon'. σὺν … μάρψας is tmesis: σύν stands apart from its participle, 'seizing together', and δύω is δύο 'two'. ὥς τε σκύλακας 'like puppies' is the simile, ποτὶ γαίῃ the same as πρὸς γαίῃ 'against the ground', and κόπτ’ is κόπτε 'struck', an imperfect. The ano teleia falls inside line 290, so the rest of that line is the next unit.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἐγκέφαλος χαμάδις ῥέε, δεῦε δὲ γαῖαν.
sentences.l: and out the brain onto the ground flowed, and wetted the earth.
sentences.i: and the brain ran out onto the ground and wetted the earth.
sentences.n: This is the second half of line 290. ἐκ … ῥέε is tmesis for ἐξέρρεε 'flowed out', with ἐγκέφαλος 'brain' its subject; χαμάδις 'to the ground' is an adverb with the suffix -δις from χαμαί. δεῦε is the imperfect of δεύω 'wet, drench' and ῥέε that of ῥέω 'flow', both without the augment.

sentences.t: τοὺς δὲ διὰ μελεϊστὶ ταμὼν ὡπλίσσατο δόρπον·
sentences.l: And them, limb by limb having cut through, he made ready for his supper;
sentences.i: He cut them up limb by limb and made them ready for his supper;
sentences.n: τοὺς is the pronoun 'them', the victims. διὰ … ταμών is tmesis for διατεμών 'cutting through', and μελεϊστί 'limb by limb' is an adverb in -ιστί from μέλος 'limb'. ὡπλίσσατο is the aorist middle of ὁπλίζω 'make ready', with the augment, and δόρπον is the evening meal. The ano teleia ends the clause; the next sentence follows without a connective.

sentences.t:
ἤσθιε δ’ ὥς τε λέων ὀρεσίτροφος, οὐδ’ ἀπέλειπεν,
ἔγκατά τε σάρκας τε καὶ ὀστέα μυελόεντα.
sentences.l:
He ate, like a mountain-nurtured lion, and left nothing,
entrails and flesh and bones full of marrow.
sentences.i: He ate like a mountain-nurtured lion and left nothing behind: entrails, flesh, and marrow-filled bones.
sentences.n: ἤσθιε is the imperfect of ἐσθίω 'eat', and ὥς τε λέων 'like a lion' opens the simile; ὀρεσίτροφος 'mountain-nurtured' is from ὄρος 'mountain' and τρέφω 'nourish'. οὐδ’ ἀπέλειπεν is 'and he left nothing over', an imperfect of ἀπολείπω. The second line lists what was eaten: ἔγκατα 'entrails', σάρκας 'flesh', and ὀστέα 'bones' with μυελόεντα 'full of marrow', from μυελός 'marrow'.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δὲ κλαίοντες ἀνεσχέθομεν Διὶ χεῖρας,
σχέτλια ἔργ’ ὁρόωντες, ἀμηχανίη δ’ ἔχε θυμόν.
sentences.l:
And we, weeping, held up our hands to Zeus,
seeing the cruel deeds, and helplessness held our heart.
sentences.i: And we, weeping, raised our hands to Zeus as we watched the cruel deeds, and helplessness held our hearts.
sentences.n: ἀνεσχέθομεν 'we held up' is an epic past tense of ἀνέχω built on the stem σχεθ- (a by-form of ἔχω), with active endings; hands raised to Zeus are the gesture of prayer. ὁρόωντες is the uncontracted form of ὁρῶντες 'seeing'. σχέτλια ἔργα is 'cruel deeds': σχέτλιος covers 'cruel, terrible', and in address 'wretch'. ἀμηχανίη 'helplessness' is built on ἀ- 'without' and μηχανή 'means, device', and ἔχε is the imperfect of ἔχω 'hold', without the augment; θυμόν is 'heart'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Κύκλωψ μεγάλην ἐμπλήσατο νηδὺν
ἀνδρόμεα κρέ’ ἔδων καὶ ἐπ’ ἄκρητον γάλα πίνων,
κεῖτ’ ἔντοσθ’ ἄντροιο τανυσσάμενος διὰ μήλων.
sentences.l:
But when the Cyclops had filled his great belly
eating human flesh and drinking unmixed milk on top of it,
he lay inside the cave, stretched out among the flocks.
sentences.i: But when the Cyclops had filled his great belly with human flesh and with unmixed milk drunk on top of it, he lay inside the cave, stretched out among the flocks.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί 'but when' opens a long temporal clause. ἐμπλήσατο is the aorist middle of ἐμπίμπλημι 'fill', with νηδύν 'belly' as its object; ἔδων is the epic participle 'eating' (Attic ἐσθίων). ἀνδρόμεα is an adjective 'of a man', so ἀνδρόμεα κρέα is 'human flesh'. ἄκρητον 'unmixed' is undiluted, and ἐπί 'on top (of it)' goes with πίνων 'drinking'. κεῖτ’ is κεῖτο 'lay', ἔντοσθ’ is ἔντοσθε 'inside', and τανυσσάμενος 'stretching himself out' is the aorist middle participle of τανύω. μῆλα 'flocks' is the word for sheep and goats together.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ βούλευσα κατὰ μεγαλήτορα θυμὸν
ἆσσον ἰών, ξίφος ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ,
οὐτάμεναι πρὸς στῆθος, ὅθι φρένες ἧπαρ ἔχουσι,
χείρ’ ἐπιμασσάμενος·
sentences.l:
Him, for my part, I planned, in my great-spirited heart,
going close, my sharp sword drawing from beside my thigh,
to stab in the chest, where the midriff holds the liver,
having felt for it with my hand;
sentences.i: I resolved in my great-spirited heart to go up close, draw my sharp sword from beside my thigh, and stab him in the chest, where the midriff holds the liver, feeling for the place with my hand;
sentences.n: τὸν μέν 'him, on the one hand' is the Cyclops, the object of οὐτάμεναι; the μέν is answered by ἕτερος δέ 'but another' in the next unit. βούλευσα is the aorist of βουλεύω 'plan, resolve'. κατὰ μεγαλήτορα θυμόν is 'in my great-spirited heart'. ἆσσον ἰών is 'going nearer', and ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω 'draw', with παρὰ μηροῦ 'from beside the thigh' and ξίφος ὀξύ 'a sharp sword'. οὐτάμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι, 'to stab'. φρένες here is not 'mind' but the midriff, the membrane about the liver; ὅθι is 'where'. χείρ’ ἐπιμασσάμενος is 'feeling for the place with my hand', χείρ’ the accusative of the hand used. The ano teleia falls inside line 302.

sentences.t: ἕτερος δέ με θυμὸς ἔρυκεν.
sentences.l: but another heart held me back.
sentences.i: but another impulse of my heart held me back.
sentences.n: This is the second half of line 302. ἕτερος … θυμός is 'another heart', a second impulse that opposed the first, and ἔρυκεν is the imperfect of ἐρύκω 'hold back'. The reason follows in the next two units.

sentences.t: αὐτοῦ γάρ κε καὶ ἄμμες ἀπωλόμεθ’ αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον·
sentences.l: for on the spot we too would have perished by a steep destruction;
sentences.i: for there and then we too would have perished in steep destruction;
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ is an adverb 'on the very spot'. κε with an aorist makes the verb 'would have': ἀπωλόμεθ’ is the aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι 'perish'. καὶ ἄμμες is 'we too', ἄμμες being an Aeolic form of ἡμεῖς that epic keeps. αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον 'steep destruction' is an accusative of the kind that repeats the idea of the verb. The ano teleia sets up the explanation that follows.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ κεν δυνάμεσθα θυράων ὑψηλάων
χερσὶν ἀπώσασθαι λίθον ὄβριμον, ὃν προσέθηκεν.
sentences.l:
for we could not from the doors, high,
with our hands push away the stone, mighty, which he had set against them.
sentences.i: for we could not have pushed the mighty stone he had set against them away from the high doors with our hands.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ 'for … not' gives the reason. κεν δυνάμεσθα is 'we would be able', δυνάμεσθα being δυνάμεθα with an extra σ. θυράων ὑψηλάων is the genitive plural 'from the high doors', with the epic ending -άων; the genitive goes with ἀπώσασθαι, the aorist middle infinitive of ἀπωθέω 'push away'. λίθον ὄβριμον is 'a mighty stone', and ὃν προσέθηκεν 'which he had set against (them)' is an aorist of προστίθημι. This is the stone that line 313 calls θυρεός.

sentences.t: ὣς τότε μὲν στενάχοντες ἐμείναμεν Ἠῶ δῖαν.
sentences.l: So then, indeed, groaning, we waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.i: So then, groaning, we waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.n: ὣς τότε μέν 'so then, indeed' closes the night. στενάχοντες is the participle of στενάχω 'groan', and ἐμείναμεν is the aorist of μένω, which takes the accusative Ἠῶ δῖαν 'heavenly Dawn' when it means 'wait for'.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
καὶ τότε πῦρ ἀνέκαιε καὶ ἤμελγε κλυτὰ μῆλα,
πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν, καὶ ὑπ’ ἔμβρυον ἧκεν ἑκάστῃ.
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
then a fire he kindled and milked the famous flocks,
all according to what is fitting, and under each her young he put.
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, then he kindled the fire and milked the famous flocks, all as is fitting, and put her young one beneath each.
sentences.n: Line 307 is the poem's regular line for daybreak: ἦμος 'when' is an epic conjunction, ἠριγένεια 'early-born' and ῥοδοδάκτυλος 'rose-fingered' are Dawn's standing epithets, and φάνη is the aorist passive 'appeared'. καὶ τότε 'and then' begins the main clause, with ἀνέκαιε 'kindled' and ἤμελγε 'was milking' imperfects; κλυτά 'famous' is a stock epithet of the flocks. Line 309 is the same as line 342: κατὰ μοῖραν is 'according to what is fitting', and ὑπ’ … ἧκεν is tmesis for ὑφῆκεν 'put under', ἔμβρυον being the young one, put beneath each mother, ἑκάστῃ, to suckle.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ σπεῦσε πονησάμενος τὰ ἃ ἔργα,
σὺν δ’ ὅ γε δὴ αὖτε δύω μάρψας ὡπλίσσατο δεῖπνον.
sentences.l:
But when he had hurried, having toiled through his own tasks,
and he again, two together seizing, made ready his meal.
sentences.i: But when he had hurried through his own tasks, he again seized two of my men and made ready his meal.
sentences.n: τὰ ἃ ἔργα is 'his own tasks': ἅ is the possessive ὅς 'his own', neuter plural to agree with ἔργα, not the relative, and τά before it is the plain article. σπεῦσε is the aorist of σπεύδω 'hurry', with πονησάμενος 'having toiled through'. σὺν … μάρψας is tmesis, 'seizing together', and δύω is 'two'. δεῖπνον is here simply 'meal'; the matching line at 344 has δόρπον 'supper' for the evening.

sentences.t:
δειπνήσας δ’ ἄντρου ἐξήλασε πίονα μῆλα,
ῥηιδίως ἀφελὼν θυρεὸν μέγαν·
sentences.l:
And having eaten his meal, out of the cave he drove the fat flocks,
easily having taken away the great door-stone;
sentences.i: When he had eaten his meal he drove his fat flocks out of the cave, easily taking away the great door-stone;
sentences.n: δειπνήσας is the aorist participle of δειπνέω 'take a meal', and ἐξήλασε the aorist of ἐξελαύνω 'drive out'; πίονα μῆλα is 'fat flocks', πίων 'fat'. ῥηιδίως is 'easily' (Attic ῥᾳδίως), and ἀφελών 'having taken away' is the aorist participle of ἀφαιρέω. θυρεός here names the stone that blocks the door; the word is later used for a shield. The ano teleia falls inside line 313.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
ἂψ ἐπέθηχ’, ὡς εἴ τε φαρέτρῃ πῶμ’ ἐπιθείη.
sentences.l:
but then
back he set it on, as if on a quiver a lid one were to put.
sentences.i: but then he put it back in place, just as a man might put the lid on a quiver.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα 'but then' closes the sentence begun in the last unit. ἂψ is 'back again', and ἐπέθηχ’ is ἐπέθηκε 'set on', its κ turned to χ before the rough breathing of the next word. ὡς εἴ τε 'as if' is followed by the optative ἐπιθείη 'one were to put on', with the dative φαρέτρῃ 'on a quiver' and πῶμα 'lid'. The comparison shows how little the heavy stone costs him.

sentences.t:
πολλῇ δὲ ῥοίζῳ πρὸς ὄρος τρέπε πίονα μῆλα
Κύκλωψ·
sentences.l:
And with much whistling toward the mountain he turned his fat flocks,
the Cyclops;
sentences.i: With a great whistling the Cyclops turned his fat flocks toward the mountain;
sentences.n: πολλῇ … ῥοίζῳ is a dative of manner, 'with much whistling': ῥοῖζος is a whistling or whirring noise, here the sound made in driving the flocks. τρέπε is the imperfect of τρέπω 'turn', and πρὸς ὄρος 'toward the mountain'. Κύκλωψ, the subject, is held back to the end of the clause. The ano teleia falls inside line 316.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ λιπόμην κακὰ βυσσοδομεύων,
εἴ πως τισαίμην, δοίη δέ μοι εὖχος Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l:
but I was left behind, evils devising deep within,
in case somehow I might avenge myself, and Athena might grant me glory.
sentences.i: but I stayed behind, brooding evil deep within me, in case I might somehow take vengeance, and Athena might grant me glory.
sentences.n: λιπόμην is the aorist middle of λείπω in the passive sense 'I was left behind'. κακὰ βυσσοδομεύων is 'devising evils deep within', βυσσοδομεύω being built on βυσσός 'depth' and δέμω 'build'. εἴ πως τισαίμην is 'in case I might somehow take vengeance': εἰ with the optative states the hope behind the plan, and τισαίμην is the aorist middle optative of τίνυμαι 'exact a penalty'. δοίη is the optative of δίδωμι, and εὖχος is 'glory', what a man can boast of.

sentences.t: ἥδε δέ μοι κατὰ θυμὸν ἀρίστη φαίνετο βουλή.
sentences.l: And this, for me, in my heart, appeared the best plan.
sentences.i: And this plan seemed best to me in my heart.
sentences.n: ἥδε 'this' is the demonstrative 'this here' and βουλή 'plan' comes from the same root as βούλευσα in 299. κατὰ θυμόν is 'in my heart', and ἀρίστη is the superlative 'best'. φαίνετο is 'appeared, seemed'. Murray begins a paragraph here, and the plan it introduces is the stake.

sentences.t:
Κύκλωπος γὰρ ἔκειτο μέγα ῥόπαλον παρὰ σηκῷ,
χλωρὸν ἐλαΐνεον·
sentences.l:
For of the Cyclops lay a great club beside the pen,
green, of olive-wood;
sentences.i: For there lay beside the pen a great club of the Cyclops, still green, of olive-wood;
sentences.n: γάρ 'for' explains the plan. ῥόπαλον is a club, ἔκειτο 'lay', and παρὰ σηκῷ 'beside the pen', σηκός being an animal pen or fold. χλωρόν 'green' means freshly cut and unseasoned, and ἐλαΐνεον 'of olive-wood' is an uncontracted adjective from ἐλαία 'olive'. The ano teleia falls inside line 320.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν ἔκταμεν, ὄφρα φοροίη
αὐανθέν.
sentences.l:
this he had cut off, so that he might carry it
once dried.
sentences.i: He had cut it so that he could carry it once it was dry.
sentences.n: τὸ μέν 'this' is the club, the pronoun. ἔκταμεν is the aorist of ἐκτέμνω 'cut off', without the augment, with the Cyclops as subject; ὄφρα φοροίη is 'so that he might carry', the optative of φορέω. αὐανθέν is the aorist passive participle of αὐαίνω 'dry', 'once dried'. The full stop falls inside line 321.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν ἄμμες ἐίσκομεν εἰσορόωντες
ὅσσον θ’ ἱστὸν νηὸς ἐεικοσόροιο μελαίνης,
φορτίδος εὐρείης, ἥ τ’ ἐκπεράᾳ μέγα λαῖτμα·
sentences.i: We judged it, as we looked at it, to be as big as the mast of a black twenty-oared ship, a broad freighter that crosses the great gulf;
sentences.n: τὸ is again the club, and ἄμμες is 'we'. ἐίσκομεν is the imperfect of ἐίσκω 'make like, liken', and εἰσορόωντες is the uncontracted participle of εἰσοράω 'look at'. ὅσσον … 'as much as' begins a comparison that line 324 finishes with its τόσσον. ἐεικοσόροιο 'twenty-oared' is built on εἴκοσι 'twenty' and a word for 'oar', νηός is the genitive of ναῦς, and μελαίνης 'black' is the ship's regular adjective. φορτίδος εὐρείης is 'a broad freighter', φορτίς 'cargo ship' from φόρτος 'cargo'. ἥ τ’ ἐκπεράᾳ 'which crosses' has the epic τε of a general statement, and λαῖτμα is 'gulf, the depth of the sea'.

sentences.t: τόσσον ἔην μῆκος, τόσσον πάχος εἰσοράασθαι.
sentences.l: so great was its length, so great its thickness, to behold.
sentences.i: so great was it in length, and so great in thickness, to look upon.
sentences.n: τόσσον 'so great' answers ὅσσον in the line before. ἔην is 'was' (Attic ἦν), and μῆκος 'length' and πάχος 'thickness' are the two things measured. εἰσοράασθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of εἰσοράομαι 'look at', 'to behold', limiting the description.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μὲν ὅσον τ’ ὄργυιαν ἐγὼν ἀπέκοψα παραστὰς
καὶ παρέθηχ’ ἑτάροισιν, ἀποξῦναι δ’ ἐκέλευσα·
sentences.l:
Of it, as much as a fathom, I cut off, standing beside it,
and I laid it beside my companions, and told them to scrape it smooth;
sentences.i: I stood by and cut off about a fathom’s length of it, and laid it down beside my companions, and told them to scrape it smooth;
sentences.n: τοῦ 'of it' is partitive, with ὅσον τ’ ὄργυιαν 'as much as a fathom'; an ὄργυια is the span of the outstretched arms, about six feet. ἐγών is ἐγώ with movable ν. ἀπέκοψα is the aorist of ἀποκόπτω 'cut off', and παραστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι 'stand beside'. παρέθηχ’ is 'I laid beside', the κ turned to χ before the rough breathing of ἑτάροισιν, a dative plural in -οισιν. ἀποξῦναι is the aorist infinitive of ἀποξύω 'scrape off, smooth', and ἐκέλευσα 'I ordered'.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ὁμαλὸν ποίησαν·
sentences.l: and they made it smooth;
sentences.i: and they made it smooth;
sentences.n: οἱ is 'they', the companions. ὁμαλόν 'even, smooth' is the predicate of ποίησαν, the aorist of ποιέω 'make'. The ano teleia falls inside line 327, and Odysseus' own part of the work follows.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐθόωσα παραστὰς
ἄκρον, ἄφαρ δὲ λαβὼν ἐπυράκτεον ἐν πυρὶ κηλέῳ.
sentences.l:
and I, standing beside it, sharpened
the tip, and at once taking it I hardened it in the blazing fire.
sentences.i: and I, standing by, sharpened the tip, then took it at once and hardened it in the blazing fire.
sentences.n: ἐθόωσα is the aorist of θοόω 'sharpen', with ἄκρον 'the tip' a neuter adjective used as a noun, and παραστάς 'standing beside' as in 325. ἄφαρ is 'at once' and λαβών 'having taken'. ἐπυράκτεον is the imperfect of πυρακτέω, a rare verb built on πῦρ 'fire'; 'harden' is the sense the context suggests. ἐν πυρὶ κηλέῳ is 'in the blazing fire', with κηλέος 'blazing' of uncertain meaning, the traditional gloss being 'burning'.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸ μὲν εὖ κατέθηκα κατακρύψας ὑπὸ κόπρῳ,
ἥ ῥα κατὰ σπείους κέχυτο μεγάλ’ ἤλιθα πολλή·
sentences.l:
and this I set down well, having hidden it under the dung,
which through the cave lay poured out, greatly, abundantly, plentiful;
sentences.i: and this I stowed away well, hiding it under the dung that lay in great abundance all over the cave;
sentences.n: κατέθηκα is the aorist of κατατίθημι 'put away', and κατακρύψας the aorist participle of κατακρύπτω 'hide'; κόπρῳ is the dative of κόπρος 'dung'. ἥ ῥα is 'which': ἥ is the relative, feminine like κόπρῳ, and ῥα is the weak particle ἄρα, left untranslated in both layers. κέχυτο is the pluperfect passive of χέω 'pour', 'lay strewn'. κατὰ σπείους is 'through the cave', σπείους the epic genitive of σπέος 'cave'. μεγάλ’ ἤλιθα πολλή piles up three words of quantity: 'greatly, in abundance, plentiful'. The ano teleia keeps the account of the preparations going.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ τοὺς ἄλλους κλήρῳ πεπαλάσθαι ἄνωγον,
ὅς τις τολμήσειεν ἐμοὶ σὺν μοχλὸν ἀείρας
τρῖψαι ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ, ὅτε τὸν γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἱκάνοι.
sentences.l:
But the others lots to cast I bade,
which one would dare with me, having lifted the stake,
to grind it in his eye, when sweet sleep came upon him.
sentences.i: But I told the others to cast lots to see who would dare to lift the stake with me and grind it into his eye, when sweet sleep came upon him.
sentences.n: τοὺς ἄλλους 'the others' is the object of ἄνωγον, an imperfect use of the perfect ἄνωγα 'I bade'. κλήρῳ πεπαλάσθαι is 'to cast lots': πεπαλάσθαι is the perfect middle infinitive of πάλλω 'shake', the lots being shaken. ὅς τις τολμήσειεν 'who would dare' is an indirect question with the optative. μοχλός 'stake' is a bar or lever, here the sharpened olive post; ἀείρας is 'having lifted'. τρῖψαι is the aorist infinitive of τρίβω 'rub, grind, twist', and ὅτε … ἱκάνοι 'when … should come upon' has the optative of anticipation, τόν being 'him'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἔλαχον τοὺς ἄν κε καὶ ἤθελον αὐτὸς ἑλέσθαι,
τέσσαρες, αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ πέμπτος μετὰ τοῖσιν ἐλέγμην.
sentences.l:
And they obtained by lot the very ones I would have wished myself to choose,
four, and I, as fifth, was counted among them.
sentences.i: The lot fell to the very men I would have chosen myself, four of them, and I was counted among them as the fifth.
sentences.n: οἱ is 'they', the companions. ἔλαχον is the aorist of λαγχάνω 'obtain by lot'. τοὺς ἄν κε καὶ ἤθελον αὐτὸς ἑλέσθαι is 'the ones whom I too would have wished to choose myself': τοὺς is relative, ἄν and κε both mark the unreal, ἤθελον is the imperfect of ἐθέλω, and ἑλέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of αἱρέω 'choose'. ἐλέγμην is an aorist middle of λέγω in the sense 'count in, reckon', passive in force: 'I was counted'; πέμπτος 'fifth' gives the total, four and Odysseus.

sentences.t: ἑσπέριος δ’ ἦλθεν καλλίτριχα μῆλα νομεύων.
sentences.l: And at evening he came, his fair-coated flocks tending.
sentences.i: He came back at evening, tending his fair-coated flocks.
sentences.n: ἑσπέριος 'at evening' is an adjective where English uses an adverb phrase. καλλίτριχα is 'fair-coated', built on καλός 'fair' and θρίξ 'hair', the coat of the sheep and goats. νομεύων is 'pasturing, tending', from νομεύς 'herdsman'.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ εἰς εὐρὺ σπέος ἤλασε πίονα μῆλα
πάντα μάλ’, οὐδέ τι λεῖπε βαθείης ἔκτοθεν αὐλῆς,
ἤ τι ὀισάμενος, ἢ καὶ θεὸς ὣς ἐκέλευσεν.
sentences.l:
And at once into the wide cave he drove the fat flocks,
all of them entirely, and nothing did he leave outside the deep yard,
either having suspected something, or even a god so commanded.
sentences.i: At once he drove his fat flocks into the wide cave, every one of them, and left none outside in the deep yard, either because he suspected something or because a god so commanded.
sentences.n: αὐτίκα is 'at once', εἰς εὐρὺ σπέος 'into the wide cave'. ἤλασε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive', and πάντα μάλ’ is 'all of them, quite'. οὐδέ τι λεῖπε is 'and he left nothing', λεῖπε an unaugmented imperfect; βαθείης ἔκτοθεν αὐλῆς is 'outside the deep yard', ἔκτοθεν taking the genitive. The last line offers two explanations: ὀισάμενος is the aorist participle of ὀΐομαι 'suppose, suspect', and ἢ καὶ θεὸς ὣς ἐκέλευσεν 'or even a god so bade him' gives the other.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ ἐπέθηκε θυρεὸν μέγαν ὑψόσ’ ἀείρας,
ἑζόμενος δ’ ἤμελγεν ὄις καὶ μηκάδας αἶγας,
πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν, καὶ ὑπ’ ἔμβρυον ἧκεν ἑκάστῃ.
sentences.l:
But then he set on a great door-stone, having lifted it up high,
and sitting down he milked the sheep and the bleating goats,
all according to what is fitting, and under each her young he put.
sentences.i: Then, heaving it up high, he set a great door-stone in place, and sitting down he milked the sheep and the bleating goats, all as is fitting, and put her young one beneath each.
sentences.n: This is the evening counterpart of the morning routine at 308–309, and line 342 is the same as 309. θυρεὸν μέγαν ὑψόσ’ ἀείρας is 'having lifted the great door-stone up high'; ἐπέθηκε 'set on' is the aorist of ἐπιτίθημι. ἑζόμενος is the participle of ἕζομαι 'sit', ἤμελγεν the imperfect of ἀμέλγω 'milk', ὄις the accusative plural 'sheep' (Attic οἶς), and μηκάδας 'bleating', from μηκάομαι 'bleat'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ σπεῦσε πονησάμενος τὰ ἃ ἔργα,
σὺν δ’ ὅ γε δὴ αὖτε δύω μάρψας ὡπλίσσατο δόρπον.
sentences.l:
But when he had hurried, having toiled through his own tasks,
and he again, two together seizing, made ready his supper.
sentences.i: But when he had hurried through his own tasks, he again seized two of my men and made ready his supper.
sentences.n: These lines repeat 310–311 with one word changed: δόρπον 'supper', the evening meal, for δεῖπνον. For the forms see the note on 310. Line 343 is the same as 310.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼ Κύκλωπα προσηύδων ἄγχι παραστάς,
κισσύβιον μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχων μέλανος οἴνοιο·
sentences.l:
And then I to the Cyclops spoke, standing close beside him,
an ivy-wood bowl in my hands holding, of dark wine:
sentences.i: And then I stood close beside the Cyclops and spoke to him, holding in my hands an ivy-wood bowl of dark wine:
sentences.n: προσηύδων is the imperfect of προσαυδάω 'speak to', and ἄγχι παραστάς is 'standing close by'. κισσύβιον 'bowl' is a wooden cup, apparently named from κισσός 'ivy'; it is the object of ἔχων 'holding'. μετὰ χερσίν is 'in my hands', and μέλανος οἴνοιο 'of dark wine' is a genitive of what the bowl holds. The ano teleia opens Odysseus' offer to the Cyclops, told inside his own telling.

sentences.t:
Κύκλωψ, τῆ, πίε οἶνον, ἐπεὶ φάγες ἀνδρόμεα κρέα,
ὄφρ’ εἰδῇς οἷόν τι ποτὸν τόδε νηῦς ἐκεκεύθει
ἡμετέρη.
sentences.l:
‘Cyclops, here, drink wine, since you have eaten human flesh,
so that you may know what sort of drink this was that the ship had kept hidden,
ours.
sentences.i: ‘Cyclops, here, drink some wine, now that you have eaten human flesh, so that you may know what kind of drink this was that our ship had kept hidden.
sentences.n: Odysseus' offer is single-quoted, like his earlier speech. Κύκλωψ is the vocative and τῆ 'here!' is the word said in handing something over; πίε is the aorist imperative of πίνω. ἐπεὶ φάγες 'since you have eaten': φάγες is ἔφαγες without the augment, and ἀνδρόμεα κρέα is 'human flesh'. ὄφρ’ εἰδῇς is 'so that you may know', the subjunctive of οἶδα, and οἷόν τι ποτὸν τόδε 'what sort of drink this' is an indirect question. νηῦς ἐκεκεύθει ἡμετέρη is 'our ship had kept hidden': ἐκεκεύθει is the pluperfect of κεύθω 'hide', and ἡμετέρη 'our' stands at the start of the next line, joined to νηῦς.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ αὖ λοιβὴν φέρον, εἴ μ’ ἐλεήσας
οἴκαδε πέμψειας·
sentences.l:
And to you, in turn, a libation I was bringing, if, having pitied me,
homeward you would send me;
sentences.i: And I was bringing it to you as a libation, in case you might pity me and send me home;
sentences.n: σοὶ δ’ αὖ is 'and to you in turn'. λοιβήν 'libation' is a drink-offering, and φέρον is the unaugmented imperfect of φέρω, 'I was bringing'. εἴ μ’ ἐλεήσας οἴκαδε πέμψειας is 'if, having pitied me, you would send me home': εἰ with the optative states the hope behind the gift, ἐλεήσας is the aorist participle of ἐλεέω 'pity', οἴκαδε 'homeward' has the suffix -δε, and πέμψειας is the aorist optative of πέμπω. The full stop is before σοί, inside line 349, and the ano teleia falls inside line 350.

sentences.t: σὺ δὲ μαίνεαι οὐκέτ’ ἀνεκτῶς.
sentences.l: but you rage no longer bearably.
sentences.i: but you rage past all bearing.
sentences.n: μαίνεαι is the uncontracted second singular (Attic μαίνῃ) of μαίνομαι 'rage, be mad'. οὐκέτ’ ἀνεκτῶς is 'no longer bearably', an adverb from ἀνεκτός 'endurable', from ἀνέχομαι 'endure'; it says that the Cyclops' conduct is past endurance.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιε, πῶς κέν τίς σε καὶ ὕστερον ἄλλος ἵκοιτο
ἀνθρώπων πολέων, ἐπεὶ οὐ κατὰ μοῖραν ἔρεξας;
sentences.l:
Cruel one, how might to you anyone, even hereafter, another
of many men, come, since not according to what is fitting you have acted?’
sentences.i: Cruel one, how could any other of the many men ever come to you in time to come, since you have not acted as is fitting?’
sentences.n: σχέτλιε is the vocative of σχέτλιος 'cruel', the word of 295. πῶς κέν τίς σε … ἵκοιτο is 'how might anyone come to you': ἵκοιτο is the optative of ἱκνέομαι 'come to', potential with κέν. ἄλλος ἀνθρώπων πολέων is 'another of the many men', a partitive genitive, and καὶ ὕστερον 'even hereafter' looks to the future. ἐπεὶ οὐ κατὰ μοῖραν ἔρεξας is 'since you have not acted according to what is fitting', ἔρεξας the aorist of ῥέζω 'do'; κατὰ μοῖραν is the phrase used at 309 for the ordinary order of the milking, here used as a moral measure. The Greek question mark ends the question, and with it the closing mark ends Odysseus' offer.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δ’ ἔδεκτο καὶ ἔκπιεν·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he took it and drank it off;
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he took it and drank it off;
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην 'so I spoke' closes Odysseus' speech. ὁ δ’ is 'and he', ὁ a pronoun, ἔδεκτο the aorist of δέχομαι 'receive', and ἔκπιεν the aorist of ἐκπίνω 'drink up'. The ano teleia falls inside line 353.

sentences.t:
ἥσατο δ’ αἰνῶς
ἡδὺ ποτὸν πίνων καὶ μ’ ᾔτεε δεύτερον αὖτις·
sentences.l:
and he was pleased terribly,
drinking the sweet drink, and asked me a second time, again:
sentences.i: and he was exceedingly pleased as he drank the sweet drink, and he asked me for it a second time:
sentences.n: ἥσατο is the aorist of ἥδομαι 'be pleased'. αἰνῶς 'terribly' is an adverb from αἰνός 'dread', here only an intensifier, 'exceedingly'. ἡδὺ ποτόν is 'the sweet drink', and ᾔτεε is the imperfect of αἰτέω 'ask for'. δεύτερον αὖτις is 'a second time, again', the two words saying almost the same. The ano teleia opens the Cyclops' speech.

sentences.t:
δός μοι ἔτι πρόφρων, καί μοι τεὸν οὔνομα εἰπὲ
αὐτίκα νῦν, ἵνα τοι δῶ ξείνιον, ᾧ κε σὺ χαίρῃς·
sentences.l:
‘Give me still, ready-minded, and to me your name tell
at once now, so that I may give you a guest-gift, at which you may rejoice;
sentences.i: ‘Give me more, with a ready mind, and tell me your name at once, now, so that I may give you a guest-gift to delight you;
sentences.n: The Cyclops' request is single-quoted, since it too lies inside Odysseus' telling. δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι, and πρόφρων 'ready-minded' shows willingness. εἰπέ is the aorist imperative of λέγω. τεόν is the epic form of σόν 'your', and οὔνομα is ὄνομα 'name' in an older form. ἵνα τοι δῶ is 'so that I may give you', δῶ the aorist subjunctive and τοι 'to you'. ξείνιον is the guest-gift, the same thing as ξεινήιον; it is the gift Odysseus asked for in the previous part. ᾧ κε σὺ χαίρῃς is 'at which you may rejoice', κε with the subjunctive making the clause indefinite.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ Κυκλώπεσσι φέρει ζείδωρος ἄρουρα
οἶνον ἐριστάφυλον, καί σφιν Διὸς ὄμβρος ἀέξει·
sentences.l:
for even to the Cyclopes the grain-giving plough-land bears
wine of great clusters, and for them the rain of Zeus makes it grow;
sentences.i: For the grain-giving plough-land bears wine from great clusters of grapes for the Cyclopes too, and the rain of Zeus makes it grow for them;
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is 'for indeed', and Κυκλώπεσσι is the dative plural of Κύκλωψ. ζείδωρος ἄρουρα 'the grain-giving plough-land' is the epic phrase for fertile earth; the meaning of ζείδωρος is disputed, 'grain-giving' (from ζειά, a grain) or 'life-giving'. φέρει is 'bears', and οἶνον ἐριστάφυλον 'wine of great clusters' has ἐρι- as an intensive and στάφυλος 'cluster of grapes'. σφιν is 'for them', Διὸς ὄμβρος 'the rain of Zeus', and ἀέξει 'makes grow'. Line 358 is the line that described the Cyclopes' land earlier in this book, where the crops grow unsown and unploughed.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τόδ’ ἀμβροσίης καὶ νέκταρός ἐστιν ἀπορρώξ.
sentences.l: but this is a break-off of ambrosia and nectar.’
sentences.i: but this is a piece broken off from ambrosia and nectar.’
sentences.n: ἀμβροσίης καὶ νέκταρος 'of ambrosia and nectar' are the food and drink of the gods. ἀπορρώξ is from ἀπορρήγνυμι 'break off' and means 'something broken off'; whether it pictures a fragment or an outflow is not fixed, and we keep the literal sense. The Cyclops is saying that the drink is a sample of the gods' own. The closing mark ends his speech.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτ’, ἀτάρ οἱ αὖτις ἐγὼ πόρον αἴθοπα οἶνον.
sentences.l: So he spoke, but to him again I gave the fire-faced wine.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and again I gave him the wine that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ is ὣς φάτο 'so he spoke'. ἀτάρ is 'but, and', οἱ 'to him', and αὖτις 'again'. πόρον is the aorist of πόρω 'give', without the augment. αἴθοπα οἶνον is 'the fire-faced wine', αἴθοψ being built on αἴθω 'burn' and ὤψ 'face, look'.

sentences.t: τρὶς μὲν ἔδωκα φέρων, τρὶς δ’ ἔκπιεν ἀφραδίῃσιν.
sentences.l: Three times I gave it, bringing it, and three times he drank it off in his folly.
sentences.i: Three times I brought it and gave it to him, and three times he drank it off in his folly.
sentences.n: τρὶς μέν … τρὶς δέ is 'three times … and three times'. ἔδωκα is the aorist of δίδωμι, φέρων 'bringing', and ἔκπιεν the aorist of ἐκπίνω 'drink off'. ἀφραδίῃσιν is a dative plural of ἀφραδίη 'thoughtlessness, folly', a plural abstract that we give as a singular.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Κύκλωπα περὶ φρένας ἤλυθεν οἶνος,
καὶ τότε δή μιν ἔπεσσι προσηύδων μειλιχίοισι·
sentences.l:
But when around the Cyclops, around his wits, the wine had come,
then indeed to him with words I spoke, gentle ones:
sentences.i: But when the wine had gone round the Cyclops’ wits, then I spoke to him with gentle words:
sentences.n: περὶ φρένας ἤλυθεν is 'came round the wits', with Κύκλωπα the person affected, the wine reaching his mind; ἤλυθεν is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι (Attic ἦλθεν). προσηύδων is 'I spoke to', the same verb as at 345. ἔπεσσι … μειλιχίοισι is 'with gentle words', μειλίχιος 'gentle, soothing' a word for speech that softens a hearer; the gentleness is a trick. The ano teleia opens Odysseus' speech.

sentences.t:
Κύκλωψ, εἰρωτᾷς μ’ ὄνομα κλυτόν, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ τοι
ἐξερέω·
sentences.l:
‘Cyclops, you ask me my name, famous, but I to you
will tell it out;
sentences.i: ‘Cyclops, you ask me for my famous name, and I will tell it to you;
sentences.n: Odysseus' answer is single-quoted inside his own telling. εἰρωτᾷς is the epic form of ἐρωτᾷς 'you ask', here with two accusatives, μ’ and ὄνομα; κλυτόν is 'famous'. αὐτὰρ ἐγώ τοι is 'but I, to you', τοι being σοι. ἐξερέω is 'I will tell out, declare', the epic future (Attic ἐξερῶ). The ano teleia falls inside line 365.

sentences.t: σὺ δέ μοι δὸς ξείνιον, ὥς περ ὑπέστης.
sentences.l: and you, give me a guest-gift, as you promised.
sentences.i: and you, give me the guest-gift, as you promised.
sentences.n: δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι. ὥς περ ὑπέστης is 'just as you promised': ὑπέστης is the intransitive aorist of ὑφίστημι, 'undertake, promise', the promise the Cyclops made at 356.

sentences.t: Οὖτις ἐμοί γ’ ὄνομα·
sentences.l: Nobody, to me at least, is the name;
sentences.i: My name is Nobody;
sentences.n: Οὖτις is the pronoun οὔ τις 'no one' written as a name, and the English name is ours, 'Nobody'; ἐμοί γ’ is 'to me, at least'. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of ὄνομα has to be scanned long before Οὖτιν, and the fifth foot is a spondee, the first two syllables of κικλήσκουσι in the next unit. The ano teleia falls inside line 366.

sentences.t:
Οὖτιν δέ με κικλήσκουσι
μήτηρ ἠδὲ πατὴρ ἠδ’ ἄλλοι πάντες ἑταῖροι.
sentences.l:
and Nobody me they call,
mother and father and all my other companions.’
sentences.i: and Nobody is what they call me, my mother and my father and all my other companions.’
sentences.n: Οὖτιν is the accusative of Οὖτις, the object of κικλήσκουσι 'they call', the reduplicated present of καλέω. μήτηρ ἠδὲ πατὴρ ἠδ’ ἄλλοι πάντες ἑταῖροι is 'mother and father and all the other companions': ἠδέ … ἠδ’ is 'and … and'. The metrical note on the previous unit covers this line too. The closing mark ends Odysseus' speech, but his telling goes on.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο νηλέι θυμῷ·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once answered me with pitiless heart:
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he answered me at once, with a pitiless heart:
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην 'so I spoke' closes Odysseus' speech, and ὁ δέ 'and he' has ὁ as a pronoun, μ’ being 'me'. αὐτίκ’ is 'at once', and ἀμείβετο 'answered' is ἠμείβετο without its augment. νηλέι θυμῷ 'with pitiless heart' is a dative of manner, νηλεής being built on νη- 'not' and ἔλεος 'pity'. This is the same line as 272, which introduced the Cyclops' reply to Odysseus' plea. The ano teleia opens his reply.

sentences.t:
Οὖτιν ἐγὼ πύματον ἔδομαι μετὰ οἷς ἑτάροισιν,
τοὺς δ’ ἄλλους πρόσθεν·
sentences.l:
‘Nobody I will eat last among his own companions,
and the others first;
sentences.i: ‘I will eat Nobody last among his own companions, and the others before him;
sentences.n: The Cyclops' reply is single-quoted. Οὖτιν is the object of ἔδομαι 'I will eat', the future of ἔδω; ἐγώ 'I' is added for emphasis. πύματον is 'last'. μετὰ οἷς ἑτάροισιν is 'among his own companions', οἷς being the possessive 'his own' and not a relative, and the dative governed by μετά; the sense is that Nobody will be the last of the company to be eaten. τοὺς δ’ ἄλλους πρόσθεν is 'and the others before (him)'. The ano teleia falls inside line 370.

sentences.t: τὸ δέ τοι ξεινήιον ἔσται.
sentences.l: and this will be your guest-gift.’
sentences.i: and this shall be your guest-gift.’
sentences.n: τὸ is 'this', and τοι 'to you'. ἔσται is 'will be'. ξεινήιον 'guest-gift' is the word on which the whole exchange has turned, Odysseus having asked for it and the Cyclops promised it; the Cyclops now gives it a grim meaning. The closing mark ends his speech, and Odysseus' telling runs on into the next part.
